column2: so the night shift did not check the Brie cave.;"## Detailed description

column1: On 14 March 2026 at 01:20
column2: the Cave B IoT gateway CAVE-GW-02 stopped forwarding sensor data after a firmware watchdog failure. CaveGuard kept the last values on screen and raised no alert
column3: so the missing data went unnoticed until the night shift checked the cave at 06:45. The gateway was restarted and readings resumed at 07:25. The incident was closed on 20 March after the corrective actions were reviewed.

column1: ## Impact
- 18 sensors in Cave B sent no data from 01:20 to 06:45
column2: a gap of five hours and twenty-five minutes.

column1: - The night shift had no humidity trend for the Brie cave. Two Brie batches were checked by hand at 07:00: humidity had dropped to 82%
column2: still within the tolerance applied by Quality.

column1: - No batch was lost and no customer delivery was affected.
## Root cause
The CAVE-GW-02 firmware had no automatic restart on watchdog failure. CaveGuard only alerted on threshold breaches
column3: and the gateway was not in PRTG

column1: ## Corrective actions
- Firmware updated on both cave gateways to a build with an automatic restart on watchdog failure (done
- CaveGuard now raises an alert when a sensor sends nothing for 15 minutes (done
- CAVE-GW-02 added to PRTG with a ping and a data-freshness check (open at closure
- Night-shift checklist updated to check the CaveGuard data-freshness indicator at the start of each shift (done
## Lessons learned
Monitoring the absence of data matters as much as monitoring the values. A sensor that stops sending is invisible to a threshold alert. The gateway also needed to be in the standard monitoring tool
column2: not only in CaveGuard. The next IoT rollout will include both checks from the start.";;false;false;;

One user entered a password; Okta blocked the sign-in at the MFA step.";"## Detailed description
On 7 April 2026 at 08:10
column2: 23 Finance users received an email that appeared to come from a known supplier
column3: with an invoice link to a cloned Microsoft sign-in page. One user entered their password at 08:42. Okta required MFA and blocked the sign-in. The user reported the email at 09:05. Security blocked the sender and the lookalike domain
column4: purged the messages from all mailboxes
column5: reset the user's password and revoked their sessions by 12:30. The incident was closed on 15 April after the mailbox and sign-in logs were reviewed.

column1: ## Impact
- 23 Finance users received the phishing email.
- One credential was entered on the cloned page. MFA blocked the sign-in
column3: payment change or data exfiltration was found.

column1: - The incident is restricted to the register administrators. The affected user is not named in this review.
## Root cause
The lookalike domain was not on the mail filter's block list and its reputation was still clean. The invoice theme matched a real supplier process
column2: so the message looked ordinary. MFA prevented the account takeover. The filter relied on domain reputation and did not detect the newly registered lookalike.

column1: ## Corrective actions
- Sender and lookalike domain blocked (done
- Phishing messages purged from all mailboxes (done
- User password reset and sessions revoked (done
- Detection rule for lookalike supplier domains added (done
- Finance awareness note on invoice verification by phone (done
- Invoice-themed phishing simulation added to the quarterly campaign (open
## Lessons learned
MFA turned a stolen password into a blocked sign-in. The fast report from the user made the response short. Newly registered lookalike domains need a detection rule
column2: not only a block list. Any change of supplier bank details should be verified through a known phone number
column3: not the number in the email.";SOC-2026-0412;false;false;;

column1: ;SAP month-end close slowed down by host memory contention;infrastructure;major;closed;false;2026-04-30 16:00;2026-04-30 17:20;2026-05-01 09:00;2026-05-06 11:00;maria.casanova@fromage-co.example;pierre.martin@fromage-co.example;Financial close jobs ran four times slower than usual. PAR-ESX-01 was overcommitted after a host maintenance
column2: with the S/4HANA and BW servers on the same host.;"## Detailed description

column1: On 30 April 2026 at 16:00
column2: the month-end close jobs ran about four times slower than usual. The first checks at 17:20 showed memory contention on PAR-ESX-01: a host maintenance on 29 April had left the S/4HANA and BW production VMs on the same host with no memory reservation rule. The BW VM was moved to PAR-ESX-02 and the close jobs returned to normal speed at 19:10. The close completed on 1 May at 09:00. The incident was closed on 6 May after Finance confirmed the figures.

column1: ## Impact
- Month-end close jobs were four times slower for about three hours
- The Finance team could not start the first consolidation run on 30 April and had to wait until the morning of 1 May.
- The close completed on 1 May with no data loss and no double posting.
## Root cause
The 29 April maintenance left both SAP production VMs on PAR-ESX-01 and lowered the memory available to them. VMware DRS had no rule to keep the two VMs apart
column2: and no alert watched host memory contention
column3: so the close jobs competed for memory.

column1: ## Corrective actions
- BW VM moved to PAR-ESX-02 and memory reservations checked on both SAP VMs (done
- DRS anti-affinity rule added for the S/4HANA and BW production VMs (done
- Host memory alert at 90% added for the ESXi hosts that carry SAP production (done
- Maintenance checklist updated with a memory reservation and placement check for SAP hosts (done
- Capacity review before each month-end close during the SAP Cheddar migration (open
## Lessons learned
A host maintenance is a change to the SAP production platform
column2: even when no VM is rebooted. Placement and memory reservations must be checked before the close window. An anti-affinity rule is a small control that prevents a maintenance from putting both production VMs on one host. The next close will include a capacity check in the runbook.";;false;false;;

column1: ;B2B portal down: database disk full;application;critical;closed;false;2026-06-02 07:50;2026-06-02 08:05;2026-06-02 11:10;2026-06-12 15:00;isabelle.moreau@fromage-co.example;marc.petit@fromage-co.example;Distributors could not place orders for three hours. The PostgreSQL 13 server of the B2B portal filled its disk with write-ahead logs after the archive job failed.;"## Detailed description
The WAL archive job on PAR-DB-01 had been failing for six days. The disk filled at 07:50 on 2 June 2026 and PostgreSQL stopped accepting writes
column2: so the Fromage B2B Portal was unavailable to distributors. The first calls reached the Sales team at 07:50 and the incident was detected at 08:05. The archive target was corrected at 09:20
column3: the WAL backlog was archived and the disk usage fell. The database accepted writes again at 10:50 and the portal was opened at 11:10. The incident was closed on 12 June after the review with Sales and Infrastructure.

column1: ## Impact
- Fromage B2B Portal unavailable from 07:50 to 11:10
- About 140 orders were taken by phone and keyed in afterwards.
- No order was lost and no customer data was exposed.
## Root cause
The archive target changed during the SAN migration and nobody watched the job. No alert watched disk usage on the database server
column2: so a failing archive job had six days to fill the disk.

column1: ## Corrective actions
- Archive job fixed and monitored (done
- Disk usage alert at 80% on database servers (done
- WAL archive target added to the SAN migration checklist (done
- Upgrade PostgreSQL 13
column3: as part of the portal roadmap (open

column1: ## Lessons learned

Backup and archive jobs are production services: their success and the disk space they consume need a monitor. An infrastructure change that moves a target must include the jobs that write to it. The phone fallback worked
column2: but three hours of manual orders is a cost the portal roadmap must remove.";;false;false;;

column1: A caching bug in the online shop release deployed on 9 July 2026 at 13:40 caused 214 order confirmation emails to be sent with another customer's name
column2: address and order content. The first reports reached Customer Service at 15:30. The release was rolled back at 15:45 and the email queue was stopped at 16:10. The affected customers were informed by email on 10 July and the CNIL was notified on 11 July at 10:00. The incident was closed on 24 July after the fix and the notification were reviewed.

column1: ## Impact
- 214 customers received a confirmation email with personal data of another customer: name
- No payment data
column2: password or bank detail was exposed.

column1: - Customer Service handled calls and emails from affected customers. No misuse of the data has been identified.
## Root cause
The cache key of the order confirmation template did not include the customer id in the new release
column2: so a cached message could be reused for the next order. The release had no test with two concurrent customers and no check of the rendered email before it was sent.

column1: ## Corrective actions
- Release rolled back and email queue stopped (done
- Cache key fixed to include the customer and order id (done
- Regression test with two customers and a shared cache added (done
- Email rendering check added to the release checklist (done
- Affected customers informed and CNIL notified (done
- Review of the release process for personalised content (open
## Lessons learned
Personalised content must be tested with at least two identities
column2: including when a cache is involved. A cache key is part of the data protection design. Detection took 90 minutes because the first reports came from customers; an alert on repeated customer names in the email queue would shorten it.";;true;true;2026-07-11 10:00;"CNIL; 214 affected customers informed by email on 10 July"

Results are recorded on paper until the database moves to the SQL Server cluster.;"## Detailed description
Since 14 October 2026 at 10:00
column2: QualityLab LIMS refuses to save new lab results. The first failures were reported at 10:20. The application still opens and shows existing results
column3: but any write fails. The embedded SQL Server 2017 Express database has reached its 10 GB size limit. The Quality team records results on paper until the database is moved to the SQL Server cluster. The incident is still in progress; this review is partial.

column1: ## Impact
- Lab results cannot be saved in QualityLab since 10:00 on 14 October.
- Results are recorded on paper and keyed in later. No result has been lost so far.
- Batch release and certificate preparation are delayed by about half a day.
- The LIMS remains available for reading existing results.
## Root cause
Under investigation. The embedded SQL Server 2017 Express database reached its 10 GB limit. The exact growth is still being analysed: result history
column2: audit tables and attachments are the main candidates. The move to the SQL Server cluster is the durable fix.

column1: ## Corrective actions
- Paper fallback agreed with Quality; a daily reconciliation checks that every result is recorded (done).
- Database size and free space monitored daily (done).
- Move the QualityLab database to the SQL Server cluster (in progress
- Archive or purge old results under the retention policy (planned).
- Vendor support case opened for the Express limit and the migration (in progress).
## Lessons learned
An Express edition database is not a fit for a LIMS with years of results. Capacity and edition limits need a monthly check
column2: not a reaction to a full database. The paper fallback works but adds a reconciliation step; the migration should be planned outside a production campaign.";;false;false;;
